title.narrative: Share-Net International

description.narrative: Share-Net International (SNI), the knowledge platform on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR), combines the expertise and strengths of development organisations, Southern partners and key international actors in the field of SRHR to achieve the SRHR and HIV related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Membership includes universities, knowledge institutes, development organisations, civil society organisations, media outlets, students and individual experts in the field of SRHR.The Platform encompasses national knowledge networks in four countries: Bangladesh, Burundi, Jordan and the Netherlands. These networks serve as conduits for situation assessments, defining research priorities, facilitating research participation by country institutions and hosting the local knowledge base/platform. They stimulate the participation of key international partners and regional and national SRHR actors.SNI aims to strengthen linkages between research, policy and practice through sharing, generating, translating and promoting the use of knowledge for the development of better policies and practices in SRHR.The main services of SNI and its country hubs include•Meetings, discussions, (de-)briefings: SNI organises a diverse range of meetings focused around relevant topics or give (de-)briefings of global happenings. Furthermore, SNI coordinates activities planned or initiated by members. •Communities of Practice are at the heart of SNI and operate in each country hub, are context specific and create common ground for members while engaging in dialogues and activities. Under this networking outcome, SNI acts as a matchmaker; promoting interactions between the members of the CoPs and encouraging them to share knowledge which facilitates learning and ultimately, using this knowledge to improve policy and practice.•Share-Net International Rapid Improvement Model promotes knowledge exchange between the country hubs, aiming to oImprove understanding of which knowledge translation strategies contribute to change in SRHR policy or practice in the specific context of each country hub.oDevelop the capacity of the participating staff in the hubs for knowledge management and brokeringoFacilitate learning, collaboration and exchange between country hubs.•SNI Co-Creation Conference aims at translating knowledge into products that allow SNI members and other participants to improve policy and practice on selected SRHR themes. Next to the development of these knowledge products, the Co-Creation Conference promotes uptake of knowledge in SRHR programmes, policies and practice through the development and presentation of narrative reviews and evidence briefs on the selected topics.•Online activities (website, newsletters) share relevant knowledge and resources on SRHR with the wider public making SRHR information accessible to all.

comment.narrative: IBP Network/WHO – Co-organise and co-finance side event during the World Health Assembly. UNESCO Regional CoP on Comprehensive Sexuality Education – Share-Net International together with Share-Net Burundi, have successfully submitted a proposal to UNESCO for the support of the further development and management of the Connect and Learn Community of Practice (CoP) Platform for East and Southern Africa (ESA). The Connect and Learn CoP is a component of the "Our Right, Our Lives, Our Future (O3)" project currently being implemented in 33 countries to promote health and well-being among adolescents and young people in Sub-Saharan Africa. The end goal of the CoP is to create a structure that allows teachers and other comprehensive sexual education (CSE) practitioners to promote best practices and build common capabilities in CSE across Sub-Saharan Africa. It should ultimately contribute to their enhanced preparedness and continuous professional development.

comment.narrative: ANSER Conference – Workshop Share-Net International, Share-Net Netherlands and Shake the Dust, organized a mapathon to launch the first global fake abortion services map. 15 people participated in the workshop which was part of the ANSER Conference in February 2024. The workshop consisted on presenting the map and the Crisis Pregnancy Centers/ or fake abortion service providers. After that, participants who came from different parts of the world, started adding Crisis Pregnancy Center from their regions in the map. World Health Assembly side event – Co-organised by IBP Network/WHO, The CORE Group and Share-Net International on the 26th of May 2024. This gathering was an opportunity to highlight global public health priorities by member states and discuss and approve the WHOs Global Program of Work. The side event was organized in three parts: A networking lunch, one Technical Panel, and a Linking and Learning Workshop. The objectives were to: Elevate the important role of CSOs in shaping the global SRH agenda in turbulent times Identify and document SRHR priorities for CSOs in research, program and policies. Provide space for participants to connect and build alliances to work on issues at the convergence of SRHR and other development sectors. Share-Net International facilitated the Linking and Learning workshop. The session was opened by the Dutch permanent representative at the UN in Geneva MozFest Conference 2024 - Panel discussion: It looks like your content may violate our community guidelines – censored: SRHR Together with RNW Media, The Center for Intimacy Justice, and Queer Sex Ed CC, SNI's iCoP on Digital Rights for SRHR hosted a panel discussion on the digital suppression of SRHR content, at the Mozilla Foundation Conference in Amsterdam in June 2024. The session highlighted issues of digital SRHR content censorship, the digital suppression of SRHR content across social media platforms, email accounts, and in search engines, and discussed mental health issues SRHR content creators regularly experience after experience shadowbanning, account deletion, and digital suppression. Global Health Practitioners Conference 2024 – Healthy Communities: Sustainable Environments Together with IBP Network/WHO and Share-Net Burundi we co-organised a session at the conference on the 28th of October 2024 in Nairobi. The event was open by the Senior Policy Officer, Strategic Partnerships at the Embassy of the Netherlands in Kenya. The session was divided in two parts, an interactive share fair session which offers participants the opportunity to learn about cutting-edge strategies on family planning and reproductive health (6 organisations presented). The exchange of knowledge and experience offered an opportunity to apply these learnings to shifting community dynamics and needs. The second part included a Panel discussion to go more in-depth on the importance of collaboration and Knowledge share and exchange by the same presenters that presented in the Fair. Knowledge Products Showcase event: In July, Share-Net International hosted the 2nd Edition of the Share-Net Knowledge Product Showcase. Over two days, Grant Alumni shared the sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) Knowledge Products (KPs) they developed with funding from Share-Net International in 2023 and 2024. This funding was provided through the Knowledge Activation Grant and Knowledge Translation Fund. A total of 10 KPs were presented, covering diverse topics such as chemsex treatment responses, forced marriages within LGBTQIA+ communities, parental support for menstruation, and empowering women to improve youth safety. Each presentation was followed by a brief Q&A session, giving participants the opportunity to learn more and engage directly with the creators. Cross-country CoP Learning exchange: In February, Share-Net International and its country hub members came together for a two-day cross-country learning exchange as part of the network’s Communities of Practice (CoPs). The event aimed to foster knowledge sharing, encourage practical application, and create a collaborative platform for networking among CoPs within the Share-Net network. The program featured diverse interactive activities, including presentations, videos, panel discussions, experience-sharing sessions, and collaboration workshops. The first day focused on Implementing CoPs: Lessons Learned, with valuable perspectives shared by both facilitators and members. This was followed by a session on CoPs for Vulnerable Populations, covering critical topics such as HIV, ageing, LGBTIQ+ issues, and the experiences of people with disabilities. The second day addressed CoPs for Sensitive Topics, exploring areas like abortion, gender-based violence (GBV), and contraception. A dedicated session on CoPs on Menstrual Health provided further opportunities for dialogue on challenges and strategies. The event concluded with a session on Closure and Next Steps, summarizing good practices, identifying challenges, and capturing key takeaways and participant feedback. This learning exchange strengthened collaboration among members and provided meaningful insights to advance the work of CoPs across Share-Net’s global network.

comment.narrative: Not measured at baseline

At Share-Net International, we have ongoing activities and strategies that maintain enthusiasm and keep members engaged in the iCoP. Members of an iCoP meet regularly based on an agreed-upon schedule, which can be monthly or every six weeks. The chair team for each meeting is composed of CoP members, supported by the SNI secretariat's CoP facilitator. A chair rotation is pre-determined and planned for the entire year, encouraging active member participation before and during meetings, while also helping them develop facilitation skills. Additionally, CoP members collaborate on knowledge products related to their interests, further stimulating engagement within the CoP. However, greater member ownership of the iCoP could enhance SNI's facilitation. Therefore, iCoPs should be initiated by groups of members rather than by SNI. The digital platform should offer the option to request the creation of an iCoP on a specific topic, thus shifting responsibility to the members and giving them a sense of greater accountability. Once a request to create a CoP is approved, SNI would only need to oversee the work and provide support as needed. Finally, implementing a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation plan with clear evaluation points can improve the CoP's functionality by allowing reflection on what didn�t work and finding solutions to identified issues. �Quote: �One of the key successes of this iCoP is that it has a specific target goal: to produce a knowledge product that gives each member a sense of ownership.� Quote: �The iCoP is a place where SRHR topics are discussed, which makes me realize and learn that the global environment on the topic differs among places and different challenges arise.�

Success Story 1: Fostering Engagement and Adaptability in the Community of Practice (CoP) Razan AlAzzah from Share-Net Jordan shares her experiences with the iCoP on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights (SRHR) for young people and adolescents. Together with CoP facilitators from the Burundi, Burkina Faso, and Jordan hubs, they are developing content for Share-Net Jordan’s DARBY platform focused on the SRHR needs of people with disabilities, while creating a space for cross-hub exchanges on national-level activities. Razan finds the iCoP experience positive, attributing its success to practices that foster commitment and active engagement. The dedication of CoP members, united by a shared passion, is key to this success. Regular facilitation practices such as preparation meetings, role assignments, and having a knowledge management expert from SNI secretariat support sustained motivation and structured engagement. To keep the group dynamic and engaged, Razan suggests periodically adding new members, allowing for knowledge sharing and fresh perspectives. Regular evaluations would help ensure that topics remain relevant to members' evolving interests. To address challenges in virtual meetings, Razan recommends strategies for inclusivity, such as accommodating time zones, improving connectivity, and setting clear objectives and timelines. Interactive tools like Mentimeter could also enhance engagement. Adaptability among facilitators and members has been essential to the iCoP’s evolution. Over time, the iCoP has expanded its focus to cover intersecting issues, such as youth and disability, aligning with members’ interests and resources. This flexibility ensures the CoP remains impactful and responsive, fostering a cohesive and relevant community.

Success Story #1: Activation grant as a sustainable and inclusive opportunity for Share-Net members Through its activation grants, Share-Net International (SNI) wants to give more consideration to vulnerable groups such as young people and people living with disabilities and advocates for inclusiveness as one of the core values of the projects it funds. In this success story, the Center for Research and Intervention for Individual, Community, and Social Development (CRIDIS) at the University of Burundi, one of our recipients of this year's Activation Grants, shares the success of their experience. CRIDIS worked on a project to improve the knowledge of young people and adolescents with disabilities regarding SRHR. Beforehand, a baseline study funded by SNI small grants was conducted in 2021 to identify the level of knowledge, attitudes, and practices of young people and adolescents living with disabilities regarding SRHR. This baseline study showed that adolescents and young people living with disabilities had a limited level of knowledge in terms of SRHR. It had also shown that access to information for this category is limited and that their sources of information on SRHR were unreliable, which had as a corollary the adoption of risky attitudes and practices. Thus, CRIDIS started this second project to improve the knowledge of young people and adolescents living with disabilities thanks to the SNI activation grant in 2022. Different knowledge products have been created, such as a training of trainers guide based on eight themes in SDSR. From this guide, a manual for the training of adolescents and young people has been extracted to provide these young people and adolescents living with disabilities with the knowledge required in SDSR. In addition, a Braille transcription of this manual has been made to enable young people and adolescents living with visual impairments to access the knowledge product. As mentioned by R�v�rien NSHIMIRIMANA, this project was an opportunity for CRIDIS to identify the needs of young people and adolescents living with disabilities in terms of SRHR, but also to realize their capacities despite their disability. In the various achievements of the project, teenage girls and young girls from two centers were trained to manufacture washable and reusable pads as part of their empowerment to obtain sanitary pads during menstruation. In addition, this project has enabled the various members of CRIDIS to collaborate with other actors, such as the Union of Disabled People of Burundi (UPHB), the National Program for Health and Reproduction (PNSR) under the Ministry of public health and AIDS control of Burundi as well as other stakeholders in the field of SDSR. The knowledge products resulting from this project have enabled CRIDIS, in its various activities, to strengthen the capacities of the managers and supervisors of the centers which shelter these young adolescents living with disabilities to equip them with the knowledge necessary to inform young people correctly. But also to train peer educators using the manual to educate their peers in the centers and beyond. Success Story #2: International Community of Practice (iCoP), a new element of collaboration and exchange between Share-Net member countries. Communities of practice (CoP) are essential in knowledge management at Share-Net International (SNI). Until 2021, the CoPs were held at the national level per hub. Various interesting knowledge products have been produced over the years within its CoPs. However, the knowledge generated was not sufficiently shared between the different hubs and other countries hosting SNI members. This is why SNI began establishing iCoPs in 2022. In this success story, Lizzie Jackson from CHOICE shares her experience setting up the iCoP on Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights (SRHR) in adolescents and young people. The iCoP on SRHR among young people and adolescents was launched in December 2022 after a 9-month preparatory period during which the CoP facilitators from the hubs of Burundi, Burkina Faso, and Jordan by collaborating with the knowledge management experts of SNI have met several times to brainstorm and establish the purpose and objectives of this iCoP. It was also a platform for exchanges between the different hubs on the work carried out at the national level. Then other members of the iCoP were invited to join at the launch. Lizzie Jackson has had a positive experience setting up this iCoP. Compared to her previous experiences in other working groups, she finds that the composition of iCoP members is very diverse, with participants from different countries. It is also a great experience to work with the members during the preparation of the next iCoP session. Therefore, this iCoP meets its expectations regarding learning about the functioning of CoPs and the facilitation of sessions. Also, the atmosphere is very respectful. Another positive point is that translation using Wordly is available during the sessions and allows non-English speaking participants to follow and participate in their preferred languages. The way the facilitation of the sessions is organized in the rotation is really good. This makes it possible to engage all members to participate in the CoP actively but also to know their tasks and responsibilities. To improve the facilitation of iCoPs, it is important to hold informative and interactive sessions. This will facilitate knowledge sharing and member contribution, and engagement. Another important element that keeps members engaged is the nature of the topic on which the iCoP will focus. In addition, the regularity of meetings every two months makes it possible to keep the iCoP active without overloading the group members. Regarding communication, Lizzie appreciates that all iCoP-related information is usually sent in one email. So members are not overloaded with lots of emails. Success story #3: Co-Creation Conference. �For global problems we need to find global solutions. But not solutions that are developed in privileged spaces, like international organisations such as the united nations. But in global spaces with people who work in the different communities in the world to guarantee human rights. And that is what this conference allowed�. (Adriana Marcela Perez Rodriguez, Observatorio de Genero de Santander). As stated in the quote above, the Share-Net International Co-Creation Conference aims to bring together people from different background and expertise to work together in the development of a knowledge product that will aim to influence policy and practice at the global level. Co-creating with a diverse group of people allows for inspiration, creativity, out-of-the box solutions and cross-country learning which translate into products that are versatile enough to be used in different context where challenges on sexual and reproductive rights are faced. During the in-person co-creation conference in 2022, 8 participants were interviewed and all of them really appreciated the exchange and learning between people with different backgrounds. They could exchange best practices and lessons learned on �Access to quality sexual and reproductive health and right information�. This gave some tools and ideas to advance SRHR in different contexts. � It is the first time that I see people from different countries, from different cultures, different continents and different areas but that are working for the same causes. And this is something very important that I learnt. And I learnt also how things are working in those countries, and that I can use to change or improve our practices in Burkina Faso�. (Zalissa Bande, Share-Net Burkina Faso). Finally, the co-creation conference is an event that brings together people working on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights all over the world, it creates a safe space where people can feel that they belong and they are not along working to ensure sexual and reproductive health and rights for all. �When you talk about sexuality in my country, it is like you are a crazy person, you are not understood. Here, I saw many people who works on the same topic as me and it was great. It was like: wow I am not the only crazy person in this world�. (Gentille Nahimana, ZenPlanet Magazine)

Success Story 1: Activation grant as a means to support breaking the silence around sensitive topics. Dr Zaid Al-Hamdan from the Jordan University of Sciences and Technology (JUST) has had the opportunity to tackle the sensitive topic of sexual harassment in the universities in Jordan through a grant awarded last year by Share-Net International. He worked on a project entitled Breaking the Silence: Sexual Harassment at Jordan Universities.Quote: �I feel happy because I have broken the silence and raised awareness around this topic.�Dr Zaid mentioned that the main learning point is that tackling a sensitive issue is difficult in the context of Jordan because of cultural sensitivity. The population doesn�t want to discuss the topic, and everyone will start blaming you and asking why you chose this topic or what/ who is behind your project. Moreover, it�s challenging to obtain ethical approval for the project. Besides many questions to answer and to meet with several authorities, it was necessary at some point to even revise the study title to give it a chance to be approved. Although the study questions remained the same, the titles presented to the students differed. Instead of sexual harassment in the universities, it was in the communities.Succes Story 2: �Kenyan LGBTQI+ voices to be heard�. Joe received the Activation Grant in 2022. The goal of the grant was to conduct research on LGBTQI+ rights in Kenya with his organization Unplugged, now known as Rights & Freedoms Network. The last national study on this topic was conducted in 2011 and was outdated. Quote: �The research provided the opportunity to give workshops to health care workers. We have actually seen some change, especially from the hospitals that participated in the research. They have seen that there's more acceptance [towards the LGBTQI+ community].�Unplugged assembled a team comprising other organizations working with the LGBTQI+ community. Joe explained that many of these organizations operate underground due to fear of government repercussions, despite their presence in Kenya. The teams were organized and began collecting primary data, as there was insufficient secondary data available in their area at the time. The teams conducted interviews with various stakeholders to assess the status of the LGBTQI+ community in specific Kenyan districts, resulting in the generation of "fresh, new data" and a comprehensive report.
